BlinkIT Grocery Sales Analysis¶

Company: Sapphire IQ | Domain: Retail & Grocery Sales Analytics | Analyst: Ram Tools: Python, Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Seaborn, Jupyter Notebook

Project context¶

Management wants to know which products perform well, which categories generate more sales, which outlets contribute most, and where there is room to improve. This notebook organizes, cleans, explores and analyzes the BlinkIT grocery sales data across products, categories, outlets and locations.

Objectives¶

# Objective Tasks
1 Understand the business and its sales performance 1.1 – 1.4
2 Make sure the available information is reliable 2.1 – 2.4
3 Find out what is driving better sales performance 3.1 – 3.4
4 Help management make better business decisions 4.1 – 4.4

Analysis flow: Data (organize & clean) → Analysis (explore patterns) → Comparison (products, outlets & locations) → Insights (business recommendations)

Note: each row of the dataset is one product listed at one outlet, and Sales is that product's sales value at that outlet. The dataset does not state a currency, so sales are shown as plain values.

Objective 1 — Understand the Business and Its Sales Performance¶

A first look at the raw data. Cleaning happens in Objective 2; the fat-content labels are standardized there.

# Product prefixes tell us the broad group: FD = Food, DR = Drinks, NC = Non-consumable
df['Item Group'] = df['Item Identifier'].str[:2].map({'FD': 'Food', 'DR': 'Drinks', 'NC': 'Non-Consumable'})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))

            wedgeprops=dict(width=0.45))

Insight: BlinkIT sells 1,559 unique products across 16 categories, listed 8,523 times across its outlets. Fruits & Vegetables (14.5%) and Snack Foods (14.1%) have the most listings, followed by Household (10.7%) and Frozen Foods (10.0%). Food items (codes starting FD) make up roughly 72% of listings, Non-Consumables about 19% and Drinks about 9%. The raw fat-content column uses five spellings for two values; Task 2.4 fixes this.

Most supermarkets list about 930 products, but the two Grocery Stores (OUT010, OUT019) list only 528–555, roughly 40% fewer.

Objective 2 — Make Sure the Available Information Is Reliable¶

Task 2.1 — Find missing information¶

In [13]:
missing = pd.DataFrame({'Missing': df.isna().sum(), 'Missing %': (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(2)})
missing[missing['Missing'] > 0]

# Where are the missing weights?
df[df['Item Weight'].isna()]['Outlet Identifier'].value_counts().to_frame('Missing Item Weight')
Out[14]:
Missing Item Weight
Outlet Identifier
OUT027 935
OUT019 528
In [15]:
# A product's weight is the same in every outlet, so fill each gap with that product's known weight from other outlets.
before = df['Item Weight'].isna().sum()
df['Item Weight'] = df['Item Weight'].fillna(df.groupby('Item Identifier')['Item Weight'].transform('mean'))
# Any product never weighed anywhere falls back to its category median
df['Item Weight'] = df['Item Weight'].fillna(df.groupby('Item Type')['Item Weight'].transform('median'))
print(f'Missing Item Weight: {before} before  ->  {df["Item Weight"].isna().sum()} after')

Missing Item Weight: 1463 before  ->  0 after

Insight: Only Item Weight has gaps: 1,463 missing values (17%), and all of them come from two outlets, OUT027 and OUT019. This points to a data-capture problem at those stores rather than at random. A product weighs the same everywhere, so each gap was filled with that product's weight recorded at other outlets. No gaps remain.

Task 2.3 — Find unusually high or low values¶

In [17]:
num_cols = ['Sales', 'Item Visibility', 'Item Weight', 'Rating']
def iqr_outliers(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([.25, .75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
    return pd.Series({'Lower limit': lo, 'Upper limit': hi, 'Below': (s < lo).sum(), 'Above': (s > hi).sum()})
pd.DataFrame({c: iqr_outliers(df[c]) for c in num_cols}).T

In [19]:
# A product on sale cannot have zero shelf visibility, so 0 is a recording error.
# Replace it with that product's average visibility in the outlets where it was recorded.
zero_vis = df['Item Visibility'] == 0
df.loc[zero_vis, 'Item Visibility'] = np.nan
df['Item Visibility'] = df['Item Visibility'].fillna(df.groupby('Item Identifier')['Item Visibility'].transform('mean'))
df['Item Visibility'] = df['Item Visibility'].fillna(df.groupby('Item Type')['Item Visibility'].transform('median'))
print(f'Zero visibility fixed: {zero_vis.sum()} rows  |  Remaining zeros: {(df["Item Visibility"] == 0).sum()}')

Zero visibility fixed: 526 rows  |  Remaining zeros: 0

Insight: Sales and Item Weight have no outliers. 526 listings show 0 visibility, which is impossible for a product on sale, so these were treated as recording errors and filled with the product's average visibility elsewhere. 144 listings have very high visibility (above 0.20); these are plausible (featured products) and were kept. The IQR test flags many ratings only because most ratings cluster tightly at 4.0. Ratings from 1 to 5 are all valid scores, so they were kept, and the low-rated listings are noted in Task 1.4.

Insight: Fruits & Vegetables (14.8%) and Snack Foods (14.6%) lead sales, followed by Household (11.3%), Frozen Foods (9.9%) and Dairy (8.4%). Together these five make up 59% of sales. Average sales per listing are fairly similar across categories (126–149), so categories sell more mainly because more of their products are listed, not because each item sells much more. Household (149) and Dairy (148) are the strongest per item, and Baking Goods (126) and Health & Hygiene (131) the weakest. Food generates 72% of sales. Low Fat and Regular items sell equally well per listing.

Task 3.2 — Which types of outlets are performing better?¶

In [25]:
def outlet_view(col):
    g = df.groupby(col).agg(Total_Sales=('Sales', 'sum'), Avg_Sales=('Sales', 'mean'),
                             Listings=('Sales', 'count'), Outlets=('Outlet Identifier', 'nunique'), Avg_Rating=('Rating', 'mean'))
    g['Sales per Outlet'] = g['Total_Sales'] / g['Outlets']
    g['Share %'] = (g['Total_Sales'] / g['Total_Sales'].sum() * 100).round(1)
    return g.sort_values('Total_Sales', ascending=False)
ot = outlet_view('Outlet Type'); os_ = outlet_view('Outlet Size'); ol = outlet_view('Outlet Location Type')
pd.concat({'Outlet Type': ot, 'Outlet Size': os_, 'Location Tier': ol})

Insight: Supermarket Type1 brings in 65.5% of sales, but only because there are six of them. Sales per outlet are almost identical across all three supermarket types (about 131,000 each). Grocery Stores are the clear weak format, at about 76,000 per outlet, 42% below the supermarkets. By location, Tier 3 has the highest total sales (39%) because it has the most outlets, while Tier 2 has the highest sales per outlet (131,000). Outlet age shows no pattern: an outlet opened in 2022 sells as much as one from 2012.

Insight: The top 20% of products (312 items) earn 36.6% of sales, while the bottom 20% earn only 6.9%. The biggest difference is distribution: top products are carried in 6.7 outlets on average versus 4.6 for the bottom group, and they also sell more per listing (214 vs 66). Among outlets, the 8 supermarkets each sell 129,000–133,000 (10.7–11.1% share), while the 2 Grocery Stores sell 74,000–78,000 each. Per item they perform the same (about 140), so the gap comes entirely from their smaller range.

Insight: The top products are spread across many categories: FDU12 (Baking Goods), FDT07 (Fruits & Vegetables) and NCQ06 (Household) lead, each at about 2,300 and stocked in 9 of the 10 outlets. 9 of 16 categories make up 80% of sales: Fruits & Vegetables, Snack Foods, Household, Frozen Foods, Dairy, Canned, Baking Goods, Health & Hygiene and Meat. These are the core range to protect.

# Category x outlet type: which categories under-perform in which outlet formats? (average sales per listing)
gap = df.pivot_table(index='Item Type', columns='Outlet Type', values='Sales', aggfunc='mean')
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
sns.heatmap(gap, annot=True, fmt='.0f', cmap='RdYlGn', ax=ax, cbar_kws=dict(label='Avg sales per listing'))
ax.set_title('Average sales per listing: category × outlet type')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Insight: Improvement areas: (1) The Grocery Stores OUT019 (Tier 1) and OUT010 (Tier 3) are the lowest outlets, at about 40% below the others, entirely because they stock about 540 products versus about 930. (2) Seafood, Breakfast, Starchy Foods, Others and Hard Drinks each contribute under 2.5% of sales. (3) Baking Goods and Health & Hygiene have the lowest sales per listing. (4) The bottom 20% of products are carried in fewer outlets and sell about a third as much per listing. (5) Data quality: OUT027 and OUT019 do not record item weight, and 526 listings had zero visibility.

Task 4.4 — Practical suggestions to improve sales¶

# Recommendation Why (evidence) Expected impact
1 Expand the product range at the two Grocery Stores (OUT010, OUT019), starting with the top-selling categories They sell as much per item (~140) as supermarkets but stock 40% fewer products Bringing their range closer to ~930 products could add roughly 50,000 in sales per store
2 Widen distribution of top-selling products to all 10 outlets Top-20% products are in 6.7 outlets on average; sales track reach, not visibility More sales from proven products at little extra risk
3 Protect and prioritize the core 9 categories (Fruits & Veg, Snacks, Household, Frozen, Dairy, Canned, Baking, Health & Hygiene, Meat) They generate 80% of sales Fewer stock-outs; better inventory planning
4 Review the bottom 20% of products and the small categories (Seafood, Breakfast, Starchy Foods) Bottom 20% earn only 6.9% of sales Replace weak products with better sellers; free up shelf space and working capital
5 Open new outlets in Tier 2 / Tier 3 as Supermarkets, not Grocery Stores Tier 2 has the highest sales per outlet; supermarkets earn ~131,000 each vs ~76,000 for grocery stores Better return on each new store
6 Don't rely on shelf visibility or ratings alone to drive sales Correlation with sales is close to zero Spend promotion budget on range and availability instead
7 Follow up on low-rated listings (218 rated 2 or lower) Customer experience risk, even though ratings don't move sales today Protect loyalty
8 Fix data capture at OUT027 and OUT019 (missing weight) and for zero-visibility records 17% of weights were missing; 526 zero-visibility errors More reliable reporting going forward

Summary of deliverables¶

  • This notebook — the full analysis, covering all four objectives and their 16 tasks.
  • BlinkIT_Grocery_Data_Cleaned.csv — the cleaned dataset: missing weights filled, zero visibility fixed, fat-content labels standardized, and helper columns added (Item Group, Outlet Age).
